1.author: St. Basil the Great
1.text: 'In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth.' I stop struck with admiration at this thought. What shall I first say? Where shall I begin my story? Shall I show forth the vanity of the Gentiles? Shall I exalt the truth of our faith? The philosophers of Greece have made much ado to explain nature, and not one of their systems has remained firm and unshaken, each being overturned by its successor. It is vain for us to refute them; they have done it themselves. Moses, on the contrary, anticipated all by one word: 'In the beginning God created.'

1.author: St. John Chrysostom
1.text: Notice the considerateness of Scripture: it does not say 'In the beginning God produced,' or 'God fashioned,' but 'God created' - using a word proper to God alone, for to create out of nothing is the work of God.

2.author: St. Basil the Great
2.text: 'And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the water.' Does this spirit mean the diffusion of air? The sacred writer wishes to enumerate to you the elements of the world. But if you take 'Spirit' as the Holy Spirit, it is most likely He who is meant. Syrian writers say that the word here translated 'moved' signifies, in their tongue, to 'brood over,' as a bird does upon her eggs, imparting vital force to them. Such, then, as far as we are able to understand it, is the meaning of these words: the Spirit moved, that is to say, prepared the nature of the water to produce living beings.
